Had a TeamViewer subscription for a few years; cancelling it when choosing not to renew was tedious and difficult. No longer recommends TeamViewer, calling it "janky as hell."

User says TeamViewer sends a reminder email 30 days before expiry, but unless you cancel at least 30 days ahead, it auto-renews and demands a full year's payment under threat of legal proceedings. Feels the email lulls you into thinking you can just let it lapse.
Uses TeamViewer on one gaming PC only to log into Windows and start Steam after Wake-on-LAN over a home VPN, then plays via Steam Remote Play. Looking for an alternative, ideally OSS and self-hosted.
Used TeamViewer less than twice a month to help elderly relatives, yet TeamViewer kept killing connections, treating them as a professional abusing the free tier. Now looking for an alternative.

Explains the installed font's purpose: the get.teamviewer.com invitation page checks via JavaScript (fontdetect.js) whether the TeamViewer font is installed. If found, it launches the app through the teamviewer8:// protocol handler; otherwise it prompts a download.

Commenter argues storing saved passwords with reversible encryption in the user's registry hive is unavoidable for a client that must replay them. Suggests the Windows Data Protection API would be a modest improvement, but says user-context attackers could bypass it anyway.
Says the real problem isn't the lack of hashing but that low-privileged users can access the stored TeamViewer credentials.
Has seen recommendations to move away from TeamViewer for years: it was once good and free, but casual users can now use Chrome Remote Desktop and more technical users Splashtop.
TeamViewer worked well until it flagged non-commercial family IT support as commercial. Tried their unflag process, gave up, and is now happy with AnyDesk.
Incident responder says they found compromises tied to TeamViewer's stored credentials. Wrote code to enumerate them en masse and analyze TeamViewer connection logs; calls the results "eyepopping."
Says the product seemed full of security flaws from first use, with poorly implemented desktop sharing, and calls it "no wonder it is a favourite of scammers."

"TeamViewer works very well, but the company is a bit scummy and the pricing is crazy." Compares it to Windows RDP plus Tailscale (works well), PulseWay (barebones and slow), and open-source VNC tools (disappointing).
Tried RustDesk as a TeamViewer alternative to help their dad, but it refused to install on his older macOS version. Supported OS versions weren't clear from the website.

Complains you can't install TeamViewer on Mac without admin permissions even just to control another desktop, unless you manually extract the .app from the .pkg. Also questions the lack of end-to-end encryption between connected computers.

An Australian retail bank locked the user out of online banking, using TeamViewer's presence as one signal in flagging a suspicious transaction. Notes TeamViewer no longer seems to be detected via the font.
Scam-baiter videos show most scammers use TeamViewer, yet the commenter says TeamViewer does little to nothing to make it harder for scammers.
A former subscriber said cancelling when they chose not to renew was "tedious and difficult." They no longer recommend TeamViewer and called it "janky as hell."

One user said TeamViewer sends an email 30 days before expiry reminding you to renew. Unless you cancel at least 30 days ahead, it auto-renews and demands a full year's payment "under threat of legal proceedings." They felt the email lulls users into thinking they can just let the subscription lapse.

A user helped elderly relatives with TeamViewer less than twice a month, but TeamViewer kept killing their connections, apparently judging them a professional abusing the free tier. They plan to find an alternative.

One user runs TeamViewer on a single PC only to log into Windows and start Steam (via VPN and Wake-on-LAN) before using Steam Remote Play. They are looking for an alternative, preferably open source and self-hosted.

A user who examined the scripts said the installed font serves the invitation website. JavaScript (fontdetect.js) checks for the font; if found, the site launches TeamViewer through its registered protocol handler (teamviewer8://instantsupport/?sid=...). If not, it prompts the user to download the app.

One user said TeamViewer worked well for family IT support until it flagged their non-commercial use as commercial. They tried TeamViewer's process to get unflagged, gave up, and are now happy with AnyDesk.

A commenter has seen recommendations to move away from TeamViewer for years. They said it may once have been good and free, but casual users can now use Chrome Remote Desktop and more technical users Splashtop.

Commenter defending TeamViewer: saving a password client-side needs reversible encryption, so a hard-coded key is only marginally worse. They suggested Windows' Data Protection API as an upgrade. Another commenter disagreed: the real problem is that low-privileged users can read these saved credentials.

An incident responder said their team identified compromises based on the saved-password registry issue. They wrote code to enumerate it at scale and analyze TeamViewer connection logs, and called the results "eyepopping."
A user said TeamViewer "reeked of security flaws the first time I used it." They found the desktop sharing poorly implemented and noted it is a favourite of scammers.

Comparing remote desktop tools: "TeamViewer works very well, but the company is a bit scummy and the pricing is crazy." The user found PulseWay barebones and slow, and open source VNC options disappointing.
A user tried RustDesk as a TeamViewer alternative to help their dad. It refused to install on his older macOS version, and supported OS versions weren't clear from the website.

Mac complaint: TeamViewer can't be installed without admin permissions even if you only want to control another desktop. Manually extracting the .app from the .pkg works fine. The user also asked why TeamViewer lacks end-to-end encryption between connected computers.
Commenters pointed to a FireEye Chief Security Architect tweet clarifying there was no new TeamViewer compromise. Social media posts claiming one were misreading a conference slide.

A user said an Australian retail bank locked them out of online banking in the past two weeks. TeamViewer being present was one of the signals used to check a suspicious-looking transaction, apparently no longer detected via the font.
Commenter: YouTube is full of scam-baiter videos showing that many scammers use TeamViewer, "yet Teamviewer themselves do little to nothing to make it difficult for scammers to continue this."
